card.hook: Forget the hotel building. The best picture at Sandy Lane is a row of bright pink loungers and parasols sitting on pale sand with calm turquoise water behind them.
card.stand_here: Stand on the public sand at Sandy Lane Beach, about 410 m south of the hotel, at the phone icon on the map. Face north, with the hotel's pink loungers along the resort frontage ahead of you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the loungers and parasols with the sea behind them. Try 0.5x to fit in more beach and water, and keep the horizon level so it doesn't bend at the edges. If your phone has zoom 2x or 5x, use it to pick out a neat row of parasols.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on your gridlines, put the horizon on the upper third line, and let the loungers fill the lower part of the picture.
card.best_time: Late afternoon toward sunset gives you golden light. Go early in the morning if you want fewer people in the frame.
card.selfie_here: Stand on the sand in front of the hotel's pink loungers and turn so they're behind you. Use the front camera, hold it a little low, and go for early morning or late afternoon when the light is softer.
card.rules_and_safety: The beach is public, but the pink loungers and beach club area belong to the hotel, so stay on the public sand. Check the official site for current access rules before you go.
card.challenge: Get a shot with a level horizon, pink loungers filling the bottom of the frame and not a single stranger in it. Patience counts as part of the challenge.
card.good_to_know: Ronald Tree, a former British politician, opened Sandy Lane in 1961 as a luxury hotel and golf course on a former sugar plantation. The original resort was pulled down after a group of Irish businessmen bought it in 1998, and the rebuild took about three years. Tiger Woods married here in 2004.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the public sand at Sandy Lane Beach, about 410 m south of the hotel, at the phone icon on the map. Face north, with the hotel's pink loungers along the resort frontage ahead of you.

selfie_spots.name: Sandy Lane Beach, on the sand in front of the hotel's pink loungers
selfie_spots.detail: on the beach, with the pink loungers of the Sandy Lane Hotel behind you; early morning or late afternoon for softer light
selfie_spots.why: A guide lists the hotel's pink loungers as a popular photo subject, and the same guide recommends early or late light for photos.

selfie_spots.name: One of the fountains at Sandy Lane Hotel
selfie_spots.detail: beside one of the fountains on the hotel grounds (the page does not say which fountain)
selfie_spots.why: A Tripadvisor member photo is captioned as one of the hotel's beautiful fountains, which suggests a photogenic backdrop, though the page gives no exact position.

selfie_research.notes: No page I found names a specific place where a passer-by should stand to photograph a visitor with the whole Sandy Lane landmark, so ask_someone_spot is null. The fountain spot is weak: the caption names no location on the grounds. The beach is described as public but reached from the south, with access by parking beside the bus stop near One Sandy Lane and walking down the path beside it. The Country Club restaurant veranda, which overlooks the golf course and sea, appeared in reviews, but I did not include it because no page ties it to a view of the resort behind a visitor. The given coordinates (13.17310, -59.63690) sit very close to the Sandy Lane Beach point listed at 13.1738, -59.6374 on Sea Glass Map. No page mentioned selfie-stick or tripod rules, and no page gave a safety point about these spots.

card.hook: This sprawling beachfront resort started out with just 12 rooms, so it's a bit of a glow-up. Don't squeeze it into one tight shot, because it's a big, relaxed place and it looks best that way.
card.stand_here: Stand on the sand directly in front of the Fairmont Royal Pavilion and turn to face back at the hotel. Step back far enough to fit the main buildings and some greenery in together.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for a natural view of the buildings and gardens. If you're close and want more of the grounds in, try 0.5x, then use 2x or higher (depends on your phone) to pick out details like planting or a terrace.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on the gridlines, put the main building on one of the lower lines and leave plenty of sky above it.
card.best_time: Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light than midday, with gentler shadows on the buildings.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if your phone has it, and hold your arm out so the hotel and gardens sit behind your shoulder. Tilt the phone slightly up so you get more of the background in.
card.rules_and_safety: This is a private hotel estate, so stick to the public side and respect guests' privacy. Check the official site before you go to see what's open to non-guests.
card.challenge: Take the same view in portrait and then landscape, and see which one wins. The grounds look quite different in each.
card.good_to_know: The hotel began in the 1940s as the Miramar, the first hotel built on this coast. The original building is now the Palm Terrace Restaurant. A private investor bought it in April 1987, restored it, and reopened it in December 1987, and it now sits in about 11 acres of gardens.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the sand directly in front of the Fairmont Royal Pavilion and turn to face back at the hotel. Step back far enough to fit the main buildings and some greenery in together.

selfie_research.notes: No page I found names a selfie spot with the Fairmont Royal Pavilion behind the visitor, and none names a spot where a passer-by should photograph a visitor with the whole hotel in frame, so both fields are empty. The closest leads do not meet the brief. Wanderlog's Alleynes Bay page (https://wanderlog.com/place/details/139150/alleynes-bay) says a palm tree leaning over the water is a good photo spot, but it gives no link to the hotel behind. Julia's Album (https://juliasalbum.com/best-spots-to-watch-the-sunset-in-barbados/) describes Palm Terrace, the hotel's open-air beach restaurant, with large white arches opening onto the sea, but it is a sunset guide and does not name a photo position. Sources also disagree on the hotel's beach: SNO (https://www.sno.com/holidays/caribbean/barbados/st-james/beaches/) places it at Alleynes Bay, while Expedia (https://www.expedia.co.uk/Holetown-Hotels-Fairmont-Royal-Pavilion.h68860.Hotel-Information) mentions Paynes Bay and Mullins Beach nearby. The Tripadvisor forum (https://www.tripadvisor.co.nz/ShowTopic-g147262-i230-k6014065-Alleynes_Bay-Barbados.html) places the hotel on the left when driving north through Holetown on the main road. A local photographer or the hotel's own beach frontage would need checking on the ground before the spot is added. No rules or safety points about selfie sticks, tripods or hazards appeared on any page I read.

card.hook: Not every great stop has a statue. This one is a working marine research station on the Holetown coast, with buildings, trees and the Caribbean all sitting together in one calm, low-key scene.
card.stand_here: Stand about 80 m south-west of the Bellairs Research Institute, at the phone icon on the map near Folkestone Marine Park, and face north-east.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the shoreline, sea and sky into one frame. Switch to 1x for the institute's buildings, then try zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out details from 80 metres away.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and put the horizon on the top or bottom line so the sea sits nice and level.
card.best_time: Late afternoon is a good bet for softer, warmer light. Early morning works well too.
card.selfie_here: Head to the boardwalk along the beach at Folkestone Marine Park and face back toward the park grounds. Use the front camera and hold it a little low and close, with the park behind you, ideally in late-afternoon light.
card.rules_and_safety: The institute is a working research site, so shoot from public areas and check the official site for park and museum access before you go. No photo restrictions are mentioned for personal photos in the park. If you get in the water, don't touch or disturb marine life, and wear reef shoes on the rocky entrance from the north beach.
card.challenge: Get one wide shot with buildings, trees and sea all in the frame and the horizon dead level. Then take a close one of just the buildings.
card.good_to_know: The Bellairs Research Institute was founded in 1954 for McGill University in Montreal. It was first funded by a bequest from the British naval commander Carlyon Bellairs, who gave it his name. Just offshore, Folkestone Reef has two flame-shaped formations called North and South Bellairs, about 107 metres and 275 metres from shore. It's underwater, so don't expect it to show clearly in your photo.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand about 80 m south-west of the Bellairs Research Institute, at the phone icon on the map near Folkestone Marine Park, and face north-east.

selfie_spots.name: Coastal boardwalk along the beach at Folkestone Marine Park
selfie_spots.detail: on the boardwalk running along the beach, facing back toward the park grounds in late afternoon light
selfie_spots.why: Guides single out the boardwalk for late-afternoon and sunset light, which should make it the most flattering spot for a close selfie with the park behind you.

selfie_spots.detail: on the museum grounds, where the Marine Museum sits on the original 1762 Church Point Battery
selfie_spots.why: The historic battery and its cannon history give the museum grounds a distinctive backdrop, though no page calls this a photo spot.

rules.rule: No specific restrictions are mentioned for personal photography within the park.
Underwater photography is allowed, but visitors should avoid touching or disturbing marine life.

sources.title: Folkestone Marine Park in Bridgetown, Barbados - 2026 Pack Lightly

selfie_research.safety: Wear reef shoes to get past the rocky entrance when entering the water from the north beach.
selfie_research.notes: No page I found names a selfie spot with the park behind the visitor, and none names a spot where a passer-by should stand to photograph a visitor with the whole park in frame, so ask_someone_spot is null. The boardwalk is recommended only for its light and sunset appeal, and the battery spot is my inference from the page's history, not a stated photo recommendation. No page mentioned selfie stick or tripod rules. Sources disagree on the reef's distance: one says the inshore reef starts a few yards off the beach, while another puts the recreational reef about 500 metres offshore. One aggregator reports the marine park section was closed on one visit, so check opening times before going. The park is spelled several ways (Folkestone/Folkstone), and the official site gives 1978 and 1981 dates for different events.

card.hook: Picture a row of pastel houses with lacy trim, tucked behind a busy road, and you don't even have to leave the pavement to get them in one frame. That's Chattel Village in Holetown, and it's a very easy win.
card.stand_here: Stand on Highway 1 on the roadside opposite the Sunset Crest Beach Club, which is a walk south from the Holetown Monument. Face south-east, where the painted houses sit set back from the road, and keep a bit of roadside in the bottom of your shot.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for a natural view of the whole row. Then try zoom 2x or higher (it depends on your phone) to pick out the fretwork and gable roofs. Save zoom 0.5x for when you're up close inside the grounds, because from the road it makes the houses look smaller.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and put the houses along the top third, then tap a brightly painted wall and drag the brightness down a touch so the pastels don't wash out in strong sun.
card.best_time: Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and richer colour than the midday glare. Take a few frames in a row in case a vehicle drives through your foreground.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera and hold your phone a little higher than your face. If your phone has zoom 0.5x, it fits more of the colourful houses in behind you. Turn so the houses sit over your shoulder, and check they're not tilting.
card.rules_and_safety: The roadside is next to a busy highway, so cross only at a designated pedestrian crossing and keep an eye on the traffic while you line up your shot. Shop opening hours and photo rules inside the grounds weren't confirmed, so check when you arrive.
card.challenge: Find the prettiest bit of fretwork and frame it so the green leaves around it make a natural border.
card.good_to_know: Chattel Village is a collection of brightly painted chattel houses in Holetown. The houses are painted in pastel shades and have decorative fretwork and gable roofs. Guides differ slightly on which side of the road the village sits, so confirm your standing spot on the map.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Highway 1 on the roadside opposite the Sunset Crest Beach Club, which is a walk south from the Holetown Monument. Face south-east, where the painted houses sit set back from the road, and keep a bit of roadside in the bottom of your shot.

selfie_research.notes: No page I found names a specific viewpoint inside or outside Chattel Village where a visitor can photograph themselves with the village behind them, or a spot where a passer-by should stand to shoot the visitor with the whole village in frame, so I have returned no spots. Pages describe the setting only in general terms: shaded pathways through tropical gardens with benches (https://barbados.org/chattel-village-holetown-barbados.htm), lawn and cobblestone pathways between the painted houses (https://www.barbadospocketguide.com/visitors-to-barbados/shopping/chattel-house-village.html), and a tropical garden with a winding path (https://www.allseasonsresort.bb/attractions/the-chattel-village). Those are features of the grounds, not named photo points, so I did not turn them into spots. The West Coast Boardwalk is named nearby (https://barbados.org/chattel-village-holetown-barbados.htm), but no page links it to a view of the village. No page I found states rules about selfie sticks or tripods, and no page gives a safety point for this site. Location descriptions conflict slightly: one page places the village south of the West Mall (https://hmb-barbados.info/en/towns-and-villages-in-barbados/ as cited from barbados.info), another next to the West Coast Mall on Highway 1, and a third next to Massy. The island guide's advice to ask permission before photographing chattel houses concerns private homes, not the shop village. A local search of the village's frontage or the Highway 1 side would be the next step.

card.hook: Most people expect a big grand monument, then spot a small white obelisk with bronze settlers beside it, right next to Highway 1. It's the sight most visitors look for in Holetown, and it's a lot more photogenic than you'd guess.
card.stand_here: Stand right at the monument, where the phone icon sits on the map, on the roadside edge facing Highway 1. Face the obelisk so the plaque is looking back at you, with the bronze settler figures and flagpole in the same frame.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the obelisk, plaque, settlers and flag together. Use 0.5x only if you can't step back far enough, and keep the obelisk in the middle so its sides don't lean. Then try zoom 2x or more (depending on your phone) for a close-up of the plaque so the words are easy to read.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the white obelisk, then slide the brightness darker a little so the stone keeps its detail instead of turning into a plain white shape.
card.best_time: Go in the morning, when a local guide says the light is best for photos here.
card.selfie_here: Try the roadside edge of the obelisk on the Highway 1 side. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if it's a squeeze, and tuck the obelisk over your shoulder so it stays tall and easy to spot.
card.rules_and_safety: Expect passing traffic on Highway 1, so keep your back to the kerb and watch your step. If cars cross your frame, wait for the next gap.
card.challenge: Turn on gridlines, line the obelisk up with a vertical line so it stands dead straight, and catch a frame with no cars in it.
card.good_to_know: The monument commemorates the early landing at Holetown, and it's a short, free stop. Watch the date if you write a caption: the plaque reads 1605, but most accounts give 1625 for the landing. Check before you post.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand right at the monument, where the phone icon sits on the map, on the roadside edge facing Highway 1. Face the obelisk so the plaque is looking back at you, with the bronze settler figures and flagpole in the same frame.

selfie_spots.name: Holetown Monument, roadside side of the obelisk on Highway 1
selfie_spots.detail: beside the obelisk on its roadside edge, near the Holetown Police Station
selfie_spots.why: <cite index="17-8">A guide says morning light is best for photos at this spot.</cite>

selfie_research.notes: Only one selfie spot is supported, and it is weak. No page I found says where a visitor should stand with the monument behind them, and no page names a spot for a passer-by to photograph the visitor with the whole obelisk, so ask_someone_spot is null. The detail for the selfie spot is my inference from the roadside location and police-station landmark, not a page's instruction; check it on the ground. <cite index="17-1">The guide describes the obelisk as by the roadside</cite>. A Barbados guide also says <cite index="20-2">it's considered rude to photograph people without permission</cite>, so ask first before photographing anyone. No page mentioned selfie sticks, tripods, or a safety point for this site.

card.hook: Picture old pale stone, leaning gravestones and a church that's been on this patch of ground since 1628. The trick is finding the gap between the trees and the parked cars.
card.stand_here: Stand at the phone icon on the map, about 30 m south-west of St. James Parish Church, and face north-east. That puts the whole church in front of you.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to fit the whole church in. If trees or the boundary push you too close, tap 0.5x. For the porch, the tower or gravestone details, try 2x or 5x (what you get depends on your phone) instead of walking closer.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line the church walls up with the vertical lines so the building doesn't lean, then tap the sunlit stone and slide it a touch darker so the pale walls don't turn white.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and warmer colour on the stone. You'll probably share the grounds with fewer people too.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera and tap 0.5x if your phone has it, so more of the old stone building fits behind you. Hold the phone a bit higher than your face and keep the building over your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: This is a working place of worship, so dress modestly and be quiet during services. Check visiting times and any photography rules inside before you go, as one visitor couldn't photograph the interior during a Sunday service.
card.challenge: Get a gravestone, a patch of grass and the full church walls into one straight-lined shot, with no leaning tower allowed.
card.good_to_know: The first settlers landed at Holetown in February 1627, and a wooden church went up here in 1628. The stone church replaced it in the early 1690s, and most of what you see today dates from the rebuild consecrated in 1875. If you go in, look for the old bell inscribed 1696 and the font dated 1684.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the phone icon on the map, about 30 m south-west of St. James Parish Church, and face north-east. That puts the whole church in front of you.

selfie_research.notes: No page I found names a selfie spot with St. James Parish Church behind the visitor, or a spot for a passer-by to photograph the visitor with the whole church, so I have left both empty rather than guess. Pages name nearby features but do not say where to stand: an old bell outside the church entrance and a pleasant cemetery (Tripadvisor, https://www.tripadvisor.com/Attraction_Review-g946443-d669608-Reviews-or30-St_James_Parish_Church-Saint_James_Parish_Barbados.html is not the exact URL; the page is https://www.tripadvisor.com/Attraction_Review-g147265-d669608-Reviews-or30-St_James_Parish_Church-Saint_James_Parish_Barbados.html), lush surrounding gardens (Evendo, https://evendo.com/locations/barbados/saint-john/landmark/st-james-parish-church), Folkestone Marine Park nearby (Mummy Barrow, https://www.mummybarrow.com/the-st-james-church-holetown-barbados/), and a small bridge just before the church at the northern end of the village (Paradise Islands, https://www.paradise-islands.org/barbados/holetown.htm). Pages also say the church is 'nice for photography' (Tripadvisor) and suggest golden hour for architecture photos (Evendo), but no page gives a viewpoint. No page states selfie stick or tripod rules, and none gives a safety point. One Tripadvisor reviewer could not photograph the interior during a Sunday service, and another found the church closed on a visit, so check opening times and service times before going. Visitbarbados lists opening hours in a garbled form (https://www.visitbarbados.org/st-james-parish-church).
